title: probabilistic-admission-bloom-timestamp-probe
body:
Goal
Quick probe: can a tiny probabilistic admission filter (bloom-style timestamp sketch) reduce eviction churn and memory bandwidth for multi-tenant, skewed workload mixes without hurting P99 latency? We want a cheap heuristic that avoids filling the on-GPU KV resident set with one-shot cold keys that cause spillbacks and high PCIe/DRAM traffic.

Motivation / intuition
- Observed symptoms: for mixed-length requests and heavy-mix per-tenant models we see repeated cold insertions into the GPU KV (rounds of fill->evict->readback), which amplifies PCIe/host-bandwidth and spikes tail latency (see SRV-5245).
- LRU alone is too reactive: it admits everything and then kicks out real reuse candidates when a burst of single-use keys arrives (hotkey storms + synthetic sampling from clients).
- Hypothesis: a compact per-key timestamp sketch that encodes a coarse last-seen epoch can estimate short-term reuse likelihood. Use that as admission control: only admit keys whose sketch indicates recent reuse or high reuse probability. Bloom sketches are tiny and can be updated cheaply per request.

Design: bloom-timestamp sketch (high level)
- Data structure: a 64K-entry array (configurable) of 8-bit counters per hash position. Each counter holds (epoch mod 256) value representing last-seen epoch. We probe with k=3 16-bit hashes -> typical Bloom-like indexing.
- On request: for each KV key touched, read k counters, compute score = number of counters with (current_epoch - stored_epoch) < window_threshold. Score >= admission_threshold => admit to GPU KV; else bypass cache or place in 'probation' (small LRU on host).
- Rationale: small counters + epoch wrap is ok because we only reason about recent reuse (window of a few hundred epochs). The storage is O(64K) bytes (or 256KB if we store 8-bit * 3 per key mapping depending on layout) which is tiny per host.
- Admission modes: admit / probation / bypass. Probation bucket is small (few MB) and low-priority.

Experiment setup
- Cluster: single A100-80GB instance (serving runtime node) with NVMe local 4TB backing, 2x PCIe gen4 paths.
- Runtime baseline: current LRU resident set implementation + current prefetch/prefill disabled for the test to isolate admission.
- Models: Llama2-13B (decoder) and OPT-6.7B used to generate KV sizes/profile; created synthetic workload mixes using recorded production key access traces (anonymized) sampled from Aug 2025 (mix A = conversational + rerank; mix B = short chat + code completion; mix C = heavy long-context summarization).
- Traffic shape: multi-tenant mixer, 32 concurrent workers, arrival rates tuned to push memory pressure to 80-95% resident set occupancy. Sequence len distribution skewed: 60% short (<=128), 30% medium (512-1024), 10% long (>2048). Zipf alpha=1.2 inter-tenant skew.
- Metrics collected: reuse_rate (fraction of hits within window), eviction_churn (evictions/sec), PCIe read/write GB/s, DRAM read GB/s (host), P50/P95/P99 latency for token generation (end-to-end), cold-insert fraction, probation promotion rate. Tools: perf, bpftrace, nvprof-like counters, runtime telemetry hooks (custom histograms).

Configurations tested
- Baseline LRU (no admission)
- Fixed-TTL admission (100 epoch TTL)
- Bloom-timestamp sketch: variants with table size {16K,64K,256K}, k={2,3}, admission_threshold={1,2}
- Hybrid: bloom admission + tiny probation LRU of 4MB on host.

Key results (summary)
- Best config: 64K table, k=3, admission_threshold=2, probation LRU 4MB. Relative to baseline LRU:
  - eviction_churn down ~28% (avg across mixes)
  - PCIe read bandwidth reduced 12-18% (most improvement in mix C long-context)
  - DRAM read down 9-12%
  - cold-insert fraction (keys that get inserted then never used again) down ~45%
  - reuse_rate (observed within 10 epochs) increased modestly ~7-11% (indicating better resident set utility)
  - P99 latency improved 6-14ms depending on mix (larger wins for heavy long-context traffic)
  - Token throughput (tokens/second) improved by 3-6% under high pressure because of fewer PCIe stalls

Observations and noteworthy behaviors
- False positives from hash collisions were rare at 64K table size; 16K had noticeably worse collision noise and lower benefit.
- Admission_threshold=2 reduced noise (i.e., required two independent counters showing recent epoch) and traded some hit-rate for much lower churn — this was a sweet spot.
- Probation LRU: a small probation bucket catches a subset of soon-to-be-reused keys without polluting GPU memory; promotion rate from probation to GPU was ~18% in winning config — low enough to keep probation effective.
- Micro-pattern: bursts that contain many unique keys (e.g., synthetic sampling bursts) are now largely bypassed; the runtime still serves them but avoids expensive GPU residency churn.
- Unexpected: small increase in CPU cycles due to sketch probing -> ~2.5% CPU increase on the host path. Acceptable tradeoff for bandwidth savings, but matters on constrained control-plane hosts.
- Tail jitter source: occasional wrap-around epochs created transient evaluations where old entries looked recent (corner-case when epoch increments roll over). Mitigation: stutter cleanup epoch marker every 1K epochs or use 12-bit counters.

Telemetry and instrumentation notes (what I logged)
- Key-level debug histograms (sampled 0.1% keys) to correlate bloom-score -> actual reuse within 5/10/50 epochs.
- Eviction stack traces for evicted keys to ensure no hotkey eviction due to admission bug.
- Bandwidth counters at 1s granularity and 30s rolling averages to see spillback patterns.
- Admission decision logs (sampled) to tune thresholds.

Open questions / next steps
- Integration risk: how to make this deterministic and debuggable under a failure? E.g., sketch persistence across process restarts vs cold start behavior.
- Parameter auto-tuning: can we learn admission_threshold dynamically per-tenant using a small online optimizer connected to runtime telemetry? (LR-3310)
- Epoch granularity: should epoch be per-request, per-batch, or time-sliced (e.g., 1s ticks)? Current experiments used per-batch epoch increments which lined up with reuse window assumptions, but needs hardened definitions.
- Cross-node consistency: for Dedicated with sharded KV across nodes, do we keep separate sketches per node? Likely yes, but this reduces cross-node reuse visibility. We should experiment with a light cross-node gossip digest in a future spike.
- Security: are sketches a side-channel leak? The sketch reveals approximate recency — low-risk but call-out to security review.

Practical deployment notes / runbook sketch
- Start with probation-only mode (never evicting via admission) to gather telemetry and estimate thresholds safely.
- Run shadow mode for 2 weeks (record decisions but don't enforce) per cluster before flip.
- Monitor: eviction_churn, PCIe GB/s, probation promotion rate, and a P99 SLA dashboard. Create automatic rollback if PCIe increases or P99 degrades by >10% vs baseline.

Action items / experiments to run next
- Run longer 48h experiment under production-mix (sampled) to verify stability and epoch-wrap behavior. (Assigned: Miguel)
- Implement 12-bit counter variant and run head-to-head for epoch-wrap elimination. (Assigned: Rae)
- Prototype light-weight cross-node digest (periodic 1s bloom merge) and measure cross-node hit improvements vs gossip cost. (Assigned: Priya)
- Add unit tests for odd epoch boundary conditions and false-positive stress. (Assigned: Ethan)

Notes to self / rough thought fragments
- Could combine with existing prefetch predictor: only prefetch if bloom-score > prefetch_threshold. That would avoid wasted prefetches that cause PCIe load.
- Think about combining usage-weighted admission where we incorporate key size cost function (prune large keys more aggressively).
- We should document threats to correctness: racing updates to the sketch when multiple threads update same counters — need atomicity or use per-core write buffers.

Relevant tickets / reminders
- SRV-5245: baseline symptom tracker and initial reproduction harness
- LR-3310: online threshold tuning proposal
- PR 812: runtime hooks for admission-bypass metrics

Appendix: microbench numbers (selected)
- Mix A (conversational): eviction/sec baseline 1320 -> bloom 950 (-28%); PCIe read 1.8GB/s -> 1.56GB/s (-13%); P99 87ms -> 78ms (-9ms)
- Mix B (short chat/code): eviction/sec baseline 940 -> bloom 720 (-23%); PCIe read 1.1GB/s -> 0.96GB/s (-13%); P99 34ms -> 30ms (-4ms)
- Mix C (long-context): eviction/sec baseline 4100 -> bloom 2900 (-29%); PCIe read 4.6GB/s -> 3.8GB/s (-17%); P99 192ms -> 178ms (-14ms)

Closing
- The bloom-timestamp admission probe looks promising as a low-cost mechanism to reduce churn and PCIe/DRAM load under mixed realistic traffic. The tradeoff is a small CPU cost and complexity increase. Next step is a longer shadow run and preparing the runtime PR to make admission configurable per-deployment.
summary: Experiment notes for a probabilistic bloom-timestamp admission filter to reduce KV cache churn. Contains design, experiment setup, results, observations, and next steps.
